title: Private tree rules and Drill Hall future
subtitle: Also: $118.15 million debenture authority, developer front-end financing policy, and a request to the province on housing at 72 Farquhar St.
overview: The committee recommended an updated Private Tree Protection By-law that would regulate trees of at least 30 cm in diameter on all private lots, down from the 50 cm staff proposed {{vote:m5}}. The change would protect more mid-sized trees, and staff noted it will raise the cost of implementing the by-law in the 2026 budget. The by-law returns to Council on April 23 for final adoption.

On the Drill Hall at 72 Farquhar St., the committee received the feasibility study. It then recommended keeping the building, maintaining it at about $125,000 a year, looking for capital funding, and later running an open process to find community partners for an arts and culture centre {{vote:m10}}. It also recommended that the Chief Administrative Officer ask the province for permission to allow housing on the site, with a September 30, 2025 cut-off {{vote:m11}}.

On finance, the committee recommended authority to borrow up to $118.15 million for 2025 and 2026 projects, mainly the South End Community Centre and the Baker District, plus a 2016 debenture refinancing {{vote:m2}}. It also recommended a phased policy for developer-financed infrastructure agreements, with new fees {{vote:m3}}. After a closed session on CUPE bargaining, the Mayor reported that Council received information and gave direction to staff.

decisions.detail: The committee recommended that Council endorse the updated by-law as amended, repeal the 2010 by-law, bring the updated by-law forward for adoption on April 23, and add new permit fees {{vote:m6}}.
The committee directed staff to regulate trees of at least 30 cm diameter on all private lots, and 10 cm on lots over 0.2 hectares, instead of the proposed 50 cm {{vote:m5}}.
The committee recommended debt financing for the listed capital projects, up to $118.15 million over terms of no more than 20 years, with debt servicing paid from capital reserve funds {{vote:m2}}.

decisions.item: Municipal service and financing agreements policy
decisions.detail: The committee recommended approving the policy for developer-financed infrastructure, phased in, with staff reporting back before full rollout and new application and administration fees added to the fees by-law {{vote:m3}}.

decisions.item: Drill Hall retention and arts centre process
decisions.detail: The committee recommended keeping the Drill Hall as a city asset, seeking capital funding for a mixed-use arts and culture centre, and later running an open process to choose community partners {{vote:m10}}.

decisions.item: Housing at the Drill Hall site
decisions.detail: The committee recommended directing the Chief Administrative Officer to seek provincial permission for residential development at 72 Farquhar St., ending the effort if permissions or proposals do not materialize by September 30, 2025 {{vote:m11}}.
The committee received the feasibility study on arts and culture uses of the Drill Hall {{vote:m7}}.

debate: On tree size, supporters of the 30 cm threshold said many common local species reach maturity near that size. They said it would protect roughly 10% more of the urban canopy, matching larger cities, and that without it smaller trees can be removed in redevelopment with no replanting required.

Staff cautioned that the lower threshold moves away from the option their analysis favoured. They said it would raise 2026 budget requests and add costs for residents, and that the Planning Act and heritage policy can protect trees in some cases.

A delegate on the tree by-law supported the staff proposal as a balance between canopy protection and cost. Staff said engagement showed many residents did not know the current by-law and opposed extra regulation, so a communications plan is planned.

On the Drill Hall, staff said the study found an arts hub feasible but not necessarily viable without public investment, given affordability pressures. Two delegates asked Council not to sell the building and to allow time for a possible private funder, and one councillor asked why this had not come up in earlier open processes.

Supporters of keeping the Drill Hall pointed to its heritage designation, the city's past investment in the building, and the long-standing need for arts and Indigenous gathering space. One councillor warned that funding it would mean trade-offs with deferred capital and infrastructure work.

On debt and developer agreements, councillors asked about tariff effects, the city's share of debt, and whether developers could appeal a staff refusal. Staff said the debt step is administrative, and that a council escalation route would be considered.
